title: India Expands Air Cargo Transshipment Reforms, Targets 80% Growth on Key Routes
excerpt: After a successful pilot on the Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt route cut transit times from 60 to 20 hours, India adds six new gateways to its transshipment network.
body:
• India has expanded its cargo transshipment network to include Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Mumbai, and Hyderabad as domestic origins, plus London and Copenhagen as international destinations
  • A proof-of-concept on the Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt route slashed end-to-end transit time from 60 hours to 20 hours by eliminating mandatory cargo re-screening
  • Air India's monthly cargo volumes on affected routes are projected to rise from 1,763 tonnes to 3,183 tonnes — an increase of nearly 80%
  • The government's broader ambition is to position India as a global cargo transshipment hub leveraging its location between East and West

A Bottleneck Eliminated

Union Minister for Civil Aviation Ram Mohan Naidu inaugurated the expanded phase of India's transshipment cargo reforms at Delhi's IGI Airport on August 19, marking a significant step in the country's push to become a global air cargo hub. The expansion builds on a successful two-month pilot program that demonstrated dramatic efficiency gains by removing a long-standing regulatory bottleneck.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=GeeH1IiRaMs

At the heart of the reform is a simple but impactful change: eliminating the mandatory re-screening of transshipment cargo at transit points. Previously, all goods passing through Indian airports — including domestic cargo changing aircraft — required fresh security screening. This added hours of ground time and significant handling costs, putting Indian airlines and airports at a competitive disadvantage against regional hubs like Dubai and Singapore.

"We are now scaling up this successful model by connecting four more major domestic cargo markets and two new international destinations. Our larger ambition is to position India as a global cargo transshipment hub."

— Ram Mohan Naidu, Union Minister for Civil Aviation

The Proof of Concept

The proof-of-concept phase launched on June 20, 2026, on the Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt sector. Air India operated the service end-to-end, using Delhi International Airport Limited's (DIAL) Transshipment Excellence Centre at Terminal 2.

The results were striking. Average end-to-end transit time dropped from 60 hours to just 20 hours, according to data presented by the ministry. Over the two-month pilot, 280 metric tonnes of cargo were transshipped, with aircraft capacity utilization climbing from 75% to nearly 100%.

The Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) enabled the reform through a revised framework notified in July 2025, permitting secured transshipment cargo to move through dedicated Transfer Cargo Security Hold Areas without re-screening, subject to prescribed security safeguards.

Expanding the Network

Building on the pilot's success, the network now includes four additional domestic origin stations — Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Mumbai, and Hyderabad — alongside two new international destinations, London and Copenhagen. These additions complement the existing Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt corridor.

The expanded network is projected to increase Air India's monthly cargo carriage on these lanes from 1,763 metric tonnes to 3,183 metric tonnes, representing nearly 80% growth, according to Aviation Defence Universe.

Additional origin stations and international destinations are planned in coming months, further building out India's cargo capabilities.

The Bigger Picture

The transshipment reform fits into a broader government strategy to transform major Indian airports into global transit hubs. Having already strengthened hub-and-spoke operations for passenger traffic, the focus has now shifted to replicating that model for cargo.

India's geographic position between East Asian manufacturing centers and European and Middle Eastern markets gives it a natural advantage — one that has gone largely unexploited in cargo logistics. Dubai, Singapore, and Hong Kong have historically dominated Asian cargo transshipment, partly because Indian airports added too much friction through re-screening requirements and slow handling times.

The minister indicated that future phases will expand the framework to international-to-international and international-to-domestic transshipment, moving beyond the current domestic-to-international focus.

For India's export economy and for the millions of Indians abroad who regularly ship goods to and from home, faster and cheaper air cargo routes through Delhi could translate into tangible benefits — reduced shipping costs, faster delivery times, and more reliable service on routes connecting India's major cities with diaspora hubs in Europe.
nri_angle: The transshipment reform will speed up cargo flows between Indian cities and key diaspora destinations including London and Frankfurt, potentially reducing shipping times for goods and packages sent between India and NRI families abroad.
